Well it was first implemented in 2008 as a $10/tonne of CO2 tax, and then it increased yearly to $15, $20, $25 and then $30/tonne, which is the rate that it is currently frozen at. The current $30/tonne tax adds 6.7 cents to the price of a litre of gasoline, and applies to other fuel sources as well, with tax rates based on the amount of CO2 that they create. Currently the tax applies to a significant portion of all emissions in the region, since it would be more difficult to apply the tax to non-fuel-related agricultural emissions or deforestation. The carbon tax has been billed as revenue-neutral, because all revenue from the tax has been returned to the public in the form of other tax cuts and grants. More specifically, the revenue has been used to reduce income taxes, reduce corporate taxes, send a tax-rebate to all low-income residents 4x a year (along with other rebates), and provide a grant to all rural residents. The key concept and reasoning behind the carbon tax, is that air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions are a negative externality, which harms other parties, but will not be properly taken into account in an individual's decision-making. This results in a market failure, where markets will over-produce goods which cause harm to people outside of the transaction (everyone other than the buyer or the seller), since the buyer and seller will be acting in their own self-interest, and not fully considering their impact on everyone else. The carbon tax is meant to account for those external impacts, to bring an individual's private costs of polluting more in line with the full costs to society. Here is an article about the carbon tax: http://www.theglobeandmail.com/globe-debate/the-insidious-truth-about-bcs-carbon-tax-it-works/article19512237/ >At the same time, it’s been extraordinarily effective in tackling the root cause of carbon pollution: the burning of fossil fuels. Since the tax came in, fuel use in the region has dropped by 16 per cent; in the rest of the country, it’s risen by 3 per cent (counting all fuels covered by the tax). To put that accomplishment in perspective, the country’s Kyoto target was a 6-per-cent reduction in 20 years. And the evidence points to the carbon tax as the major driver of these regional gains. >Further, while some had predicted that the tax shift would hurt the province’s economy, in fact, the region’s GDP has slightly outperformed the rest of the country’s since 2008. And here's an academic article about the carbon tax and a related proposal, from a university professor, considered from more of a political angle: http://www.standupeconomist.com/pdf/carbon/2012.Harrison.TaleofTwoTaxes.pdf Let me know if you have any other questions, and I'll see if I have an answer.

Wards vs At-Large voting is an interesting question, and there's definite pros and cons to each.  Wards allow for representation closer to the people, but potentially leads to councillors to focus too much on the interests of their neighbourhood and ignore the impact on others (and thus more NIMBYism and political fights between different neighbourhoods).  At-Large voting allows councillors to consider the big picture instead of just the needs of their own neighbourhood, but it also makes it more difficult for independents or lesser known people to get elected through grass-roots campaigns, and means less direct representation for people. I really don't know what I'd prefer.  I currently like the way the current system reduces the amount of neighbourhood politics and allows councillors to focus on the big-picture and get things done, but I do see real merits in having a ward-based system, and understand the concerns that the current system makes local politics overwhelming for most voters (how can they possibly have an opinion about so many candidates?), and thus has negative impacts on voter engagement and their representation. Interestingly, there have been 5 referendums/plebiscites on this topic since 1970: >1973: 59 per cent of voters chose to keep the at-large system. >1978: 52 per cent voted in favour of reinstating a ward system. However, the provincial government's amendments to the Vancouver Charter, the legislation that governs the city, specified that Vancouver's electoral system could only be changed with a 60 per cent majority vote in a referendum. >1988: 56 per cent majority in favour of wards, which was not enough to meet the 60 per cent required. >1996: 59 per cent voted in favour of keeping the at-large system. >2004: 54 per voted opposed to adopting a ward system. http://searcharchives.vancouver.ca/vancouver-b-c-electoral-reform-commission

>I find it interesting that most people arguing against a referendum are basically arguing against democracy. Not at all.  Voting for a representative is very different from voting on a specific topic. Most people are interested and knowledgeable about *some* topics, but very few people are interested and knowledgeable about *every* topic.  When voting for political parties and representatives, people can use the issues that they know and care most about to decide which party best matches their views and values. So for example, if I know lots about economic and environmental policy, but only have a shallow understanding of foreign policy, it's okay because I can judge the parties based on their economic and environmental policies, which are issues that I do understand. However with a referendum, we're relying on *everyone* to be knowledgeable, interested, and informed about the same topic.  If it's a topic with any complexity (like electoral reform), then that won't necessarily work very well, because let's be honest: most people are not going to approach the topic with an open mind and spend 3+ hours independently researching it, and weighing the tradeoffs and potential implications.  Most will hear about it on the news a few times, hear an argument that they like, and vote accordingly.  This also makes it very easy for many people to be convinced by misleading information, because they're not experts on the topic, and most people don't have the time or interest to develop a very thorough understanding of the topic before voting.

Basically the countries in a regional free-movement area have no border controls between themselves, so people and goods can move freely between them without any waits, and without needing to bring a passport.  So for example, you can drive or take a train from one country to another to another to another without going through any border stops, or you can fly between those countries without going through customs.  It also speeds up goods movement, since trucks and freight trains don't have to wait in border lines and get searched every time they cross a national border. However there are still border stops and customs for entering or leaving the area (so going from a country in one continent to a country in another continent you still need a passport and must clear customs, obviously). The upsides are easier travel, more efficient trade, etc.  Downsides are that each country has less control over who or what goods enter their country, so they have to establish some common rules and regulations that apply to all countries in the area, and they also have to count of the other countries in the area to be secure.
